newsitem.title: UK: The Proteus Column - Lloyd's conference.
newsitem.headline: The Proteus Column - Lloyd's conference.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Yesterday's announcement of a Lloyd's professional indemnity conference could mark a fundamental change in the way the market goes out and develops business.
Firstly, it is a market-led initiative which evolved from regular meetings of professional indemnity underwriters. Until now, Lloyd's itself was the prime mover in any market-wide initiatives.

Lloyd's chairman Sir David Rowland has been spearheading almost single-handed the market's strategy to win new business and restore its tarnished reputation in the wake of record losses and near collapse.
The organisation of next week's conference is a joint effort between the Lloyd's marketing department and professional indemnity underwriters at Lloyd's.

In another significant departure, the conference is being funded by the users rather than by Lloyd's centrally. In the longer term, Lloyd's hopes that more of its central services will be paid for directly.
The conference also signifies the underwriters' desire to get closer to their clients with a view to expanding their business by promoting Lloyd's collectively.
As one Lloyd's professional said, "We have a tremendous knowledge base, but something we don't do very well is talk to clients."
Underwriters need to get across the message that a Lloyd's policy provides a complete risk management service, not just a promise to pay out if something goes wrong, he said.
In Lloyd's subscription market policyholders also benefit from the experience of several underwriters looking at each risk, he added.
If, as Lloyd's hopes, this is the first of many such conferences, it could mean more pressure on the already struggling broker market.
By getting closer to their clients, professional indemnity underwriters hope to be able to add value. This will inevitably involve some encroachment on the domain of brokers.
It could also mean that gone are the days when Lloyd's underwriters regarded brokers as people whose main role was to act as a barrier between them and the insured.

Another question the conference raises is its location -- why Alexandra Palace? Most business conferences are held in one of the large hotels in central London. Alexandra Palace is a large conference venue, but well away from the city centre.

The answer, according to Lloyd's, is that the 350 delegates wanted somewhere different, with a little more glamour and interest than an international hotel. Since most of them are travelling from the U.S., a few extra miles out to Ally Pally, as the venue is known locally, probably won't bother them.
